title: High Expectations, High Support
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt presents a case study of Lingfield Primary School -- where approximately 40% of pupils are classified as vulnerable -- to demonstrate what high expectations with equally high support looks like in practice, rather than as a leadership slogan. The school achieves 97% of pupils on track in phonics, a figure that would be notable at any school but is remarkable given the demographic profile. Myatt traces the specific mechanisms through which those results are produced: discovery bags distributed beginning in nursery to build early vocabulary and handle object relationship; phonics expectations made explicit through structured parent workshops followed up in the classroom; before- and after-school reading sessions for pupils who need additional exposure; and consistent teacher practice built around making the implicit explicit rather than assuming children will absorb norms through proximity. The core argument, which Myatt returns to repeatedly, is that equity is achieved by removing barriers rather than lowering the bar -- that the schools which serve vulnerable pupils best are those that hold the standard constant and vary the support to match individual need. She closes with a practical observation that functions as both research summary and practitioner challenge: ten to fifteen minutes of focused, consistent reading practice, done reliably, is transformational -- not because any single session changes a child, but because the compound effect over months is larger than most educators intuitively account for.
points: Lingfield Primary achieves 97% phonics on track with a 40% vulnerable-pupil population -- evidence that high-demographic challenge and high academic expectation are not in tension when support is deliberately engineered.
Discovery bags starting in nursery address the vocabulary-gap problem at its earliest point rather than waiting for formal schooling to reveal it.
Parent workshops that make phonics expectations explicit -- and then follow up in the classroom -- create the home-school alignment that low-income families are often assumed to be unable to provide.
Equity is achieved by removing barriers rather than lowering the bar: the standard stays constant and the support varies, which is the inversion of deficit-model accommodation.
Ten to fifteen minutes of consistent, focused reading practice compounds: the practitioner challenge is resisting the intuition that such small daily increments are insufficient.
quotes: Forty percent of their pupils are classified as vulnerable. Ninety-seven percent are on track in phonics. Those two facts do not coexist by accident. They coexist because someone decided that the second fact was not contingent on the first.
The discovery bags go home from nursery. Not Year 1, not Reception -- nursery. Because the vocabulary gap does not wait for formal schooling to open, and neither should the school.

The workshops make explicit what many schools leave implicit: here is what phonics learning looks like, here is what you are listening for, here is what you can do at home tonight. That is not a soft add-on. That is closing a support gap.

Equity in this school does not mean adjusting expectations downward for children who arrive with less. It means adjusting support upward until the expectation is achievable. The bar stays. The scaffold changes.

Ten to fifteen minutes a day, consistently. That is the finding. Not an intervention programme, not an expensive purchase, not a structural overhaul. Consistent, focused reading practice, every day. The compound effect over a year is larger than most teachers intuitively believe.
